newsitem.title: USA: FCC deals Ameritech long-distance setback.
newsitem.headline: FCC deals Ameritech long-distance setback.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Communications Commission on Friday dealt a blow to Ameritech Corp's bid to enter the $80 billion long-distance phone business, saying it would refuse to consider key evidence submitted by Ameritech as part of its application.

The Federal Communications Commission issued the decision after a phone industry trade group charged that some of the documents Chicago-based Ameritech submitted in support of its bid to offer long-distance service from Michigan were flawed.
Ameritech must decide by Tuesday whether to risk FCC rejection by proceeding without the documents, which the company had claimed showed that it had opened its local phone network to AT&T Corp.

Or, it could suffer more delays by withdrawing the application and submitting a new one, thus restarting the clock governing the 90-day FCC approval process spelled out under last year's communications act.
Ameritech asked the FCC on Jan. 2 for permission to offer long-distance service to residents in Michigan, one of five Midwestern states in which it provides local service.

Ameritech's latest problems began after the Association for Local Telecommunications Service, or ALTS, asked the FCC to force Ameritech to strike the AT&T document from its application, saying that the agreement with AT&T was not valid.
ALTS represents local phone companies that serve mainly businesses.

Under the new telecom act, Ameritech and the other regional Baby Bells must prove to regulators that they have opened their local phone monopolies to new competitors before gaining access to the long-distance market.
The FCC noted that Michigan regulators said they had not yet approved Ameritech's "interconnection" agreement with AT&T at the time it made its most recent filing.
Ameritech first asked the FCC on Jan. 2 for permission to offer long-distance service to residents in Michigan, one of five Midwestern states in which it provides local service.

The company is the first regional Baby Bell to seek approval under the communications act. Ironically, Ameritech on Wednesday won the endorsement of regulators in Michigan, although the FCC has final say in the matter.
This is not the first problem Ameritech has encountered.

After filing its initial request with the FCC, Ameritech had to amend it with an additional 1,500 pages of documents after rivals discovered numerous inaccuracies. That refiling restarted the approval clock.
